title: Laundromat Machine Count
story: You are opening a laundromat that works by reservation. Customers book a washing machine for a time window, in minutes after opening: [10, 40] means they load at minute 10 and the machine is free again at minute 40. A machine that frees up at minute 40 can take a new load that starts at minute 40.
Machines are expensive. Looking at a busy Saturday's reservations, how few machines could have served every customer on time?
task: Write machinesNeeded(loads). Each load is [start, end] with start < end. Return the minimum number of machines so that every load can run on some machine, and no machine runs two loads at once.
A load ending at time t and another starting at time t can share a machine. An empty list needs 0 machines.

examples.explanation: From minute 10 to 40 two loads run at once, so you need at least 2 machines. And 2 is enough: machine A runs [0, 45] then [50, 95]; machine B runs [10, 40] then [40, 70].
Each load starts exactly when the previous one ends, so one machine handles all three back to back.

hints: In the first example, pick any minute and count how many loads are running then. What is the largest count you can find, and how does it relate to the answer?
You can never use fewer machines than the most loads running at the same moment. It turns out you never need more, either. So the real question is: what is the peak number of loads in progress?

The count only changes when a load starts (+1) or ends (-1). If you look at those moments in time order, you can track the count as you go. What should happen when an end and a start share the same minute?

Sort all start times, and separately all end times. Walk through the starts in order; before counting a start, release every load whose end ≤ that start (one pointer into the sorted ends). Track the running count and its maximum. An end at the same minute is released first, because touching loads can share a machine.
bruteForce: For every load's start time, count how many loads are running at that moment (start ≤ t < end) by scanning the whole list. The peak count is the answer, because the busiest moment is always some load's start.
That is n checks of n loads each: O(n²), about 100 million comparisons for 10,000 loads. The scan recounts the same loads again and again; sorting lets you keep a running count instead.

js: * @return {number} fewest machines that serve every load

tests.note: one long load, short ones reuse a second machine
counting everything that overlaps one load gives 5
machines handed over at the same minute

js: const starts = loads.map(l => l[0]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
const ends = loads.map(l => l[1]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
// Free every machine whose load is done by now.
py: starts = sorted(s for s, _ in loads)
ends = sorted(e for _, e in loads)
# Free every machine whose load is done by now.
walkthrough: The answer is the largest number of loads running at the same moment. Fewer machines cannot work at that moment, and that many always suffice, because you can hand each new load any machine that is free. To find the peak, sweep through time: a start adds one running load, an end removes one.
• Start 40. The end at 40 is ≤ 40, so release it first: running 1. Then start: running 2. Peak stays 2.
• Start 50. The end at 45 is ≤ 50: release, running 1. Start: running 2. Answer: 2.

Releasing ends with ≤ before counting the start is what lets touching loads share a machine. With < you would report 3 for loads that only hand over a machine. The inner loop never runs past the end of ends: when a start is being counted, that load's own end is still waiting, so there is always an end greater than the current start.
solution.timeWhy: Two sorts; the sweep moves each pointer through its list once.
solution.spaceWhy: The two sorted lists of times.
solution.takeaway: To find how many intervals are active at the busiest moment, split them into start events and end events, sort, and sweep with a running count. A min-heap of end times does the same job and also tells you which machine to reuse.
